title: Hinduism: namaste
hook: the greeting bows to the divine in the other person
tomorrow: Hinduism: the lamp and the flower

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma yoga, Krishna's advice to Arjuna on the battlefield. Your line was the act, not the fruit. Day two hundred thirty-six.

A T-shirt, a doormat, a coffee mug, the last minute of a yoga class with hands pressed together: this word has traveled a long way from home. In Delhi or Kathmandu, it isn't a spiritual slogan. It's hello. It's what people say to an aunt, a neighbor, the shopkeeper on the corner, the guest at the door. And inside that everyday hello is a small act of honor. The word is namaste.
screen: `THE END OF A YOGA CLASS.` → `IN DELHI, IT'S HELLO.` → `NAMASTE.`

segments.voice: Namaste is Sanskrit, two small words joined. Namas means a bow, a bending, an act of honor. Te means to you. So namaste, word for word, is a bow to you. I bow to you. Usually it comes with a gesture: palms pressed together in front of the heart, fingers pointing up, often with a small bow of the head. The gesture has its own name, anjali, an offering of joined hands. A little more formally, the greeting is namaskar. Now, the phrase you may have heard: the divine in me bows to the divine in you. That's a popular explanation, especially in yoga studios, and it isn't in the word itself. But it isn't made up out of nothing, either. Some Hindu teachers do explain the gesture this way: bowing to another person honors the sacred present in them, an idea that echoes the salt in the water two days ago. So there are two honest layers. The literal one: I bow to you. The meaning some Hindus hear inside it: I honor what's holy in you. Either way, look at what the greeting does. It doesn't grab, it doesn't shake, it doesn't hug without asking. It lowers the head a little. It puts both hands where they can't hold anything. It makes a small space of respect between two people. A handshake says, I'm here. Namaste says, I see you, and I bow.
screen: `NAMAS: A BOW. TE: TO YOU.` · `PALMS TOGETHER AT THE HEART.` · `THE DIVINE IN YOU: A GLOSS.` · `A SMALL SPACE OF RESPECT.` · then, large: `I BOW TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring your palms together in front of your chest and feel the two hands meet. Picture someone you'll see today, even someone who irritates you a little, and lower your head slightly toward them in your mind. Let the words be simply: I bow to you.
Namaste. Sanskrit for a bow to you, with palms together at the heart; some Hindus hear in it an honor to the sacred in the other. Today's word.
Your line: I bow to you. Any hello can carry a little of that bow. That's day two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Across India and Nepal, namaste or namaskar with palms joined is an everyday greeting and farewell, used with elders, guests and strangers, and it is also offered before images of the gods.
